draft.title: The emperor and the shogun
card: The head of Japan's royal family. Under the shoguns he kept a religious and ceremonial role, such as leading rituals, but he did not run the country.
A military ruler who held real power in Japan. He controlled the armies and made the big decisions about how the country was run.
In 1192 the emperor gave Minamoto no Yoritomo the title of shogun. From then, shoguns held real power in Japan.
The emperor stayed in place and was still treated with great respect. Shoguns ruled in his name, so power and status were split between two people.
draft.remember: The shogun ruled Japan. The emperor stayed on as a religious and ceremonial figure.

a.q: From 1192, which description best fits the shogun's place in Japan?
opts: A military ruler who held real power
A priest who led the country's religion
A noble who advised the emperor in court
A foreign envoy who traded for Japan
a.why: The shogun was a military ruler who controlled the armies and held real power. He was not mainly a priest, because the religious and ceremonial role stayed with the emperor.
a.clue: Think about who held real power, not who held the highest status.

b.q: A shogun orders an army to march against a rebel lord. The emperor holds a ritual at his palace. What does this show about Japan at this time?
opts: The shogun held real power and the emperor was ceremonial
The emperor held real power and the shogun was a priest
The emperor and shogun had no place in government
The shogun had removed the emperor from his position
b.why: Giving orders to an army shows real power, which belonged to the shogun. The emperor's ritual fits his religious and ceremonial role. The emperor was not removed, as he stayed in place and was still respected.
b.clue: Match each action to the kind of role it shows.

a.best: A military ruler who held real power

b.best: The shogun held real power and the emperor was ceremonial
